faqs.question: What is ANSI/TIA-942?
faqs.answer: ANSI/TIA-942 is the Telecommunications Industry Association standard for data center infrastructure. It covers the layout of spaces, cabling, and electrical, mechanical and other infrastructure, and defines rated reliability levels. Many owners and designers use it as the baseline for new facilities.

faqs.question: What is the difference between N+1 and 2N redundancy?
faqs.answer: N is the capacity needed to carry the load. N+1 adds one extra component, such as one spare UPS module or chiller. 2N provides two complete, independent systems, each able to carry the full load. 2N costs more but can tolerate the loss of an entire path.

faqs.question: What does a typical data center power chain look like?
faqs.answer: Utility power enters through medium-voltage switchgear and is stepped down by transformers. It passes through switchboards to UPS systems, which provide ride-through during outages, then to PDUs and remote power panels, and finally to rack PDUs and servers. Generators back up the utility.

faqs.question: What is distributed redundancy?
faqs.answer: Distributed redundant designs, sometimes called 3-to-make-2 or 4-to-make-3, spread load across several UPS systems so that the failure of one can be absorbed by the others. They can offer high availability with less idle equipment than a full 2N design.

faqs.answer: Electricians, power engineers, facilities technicians and project engineers who work on or specify critical power systems, plus operations staff who want a full picture of the electrical infrastructure they rely on.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a CRAC and a CRAH?
faqs.answer: A CRAC (computer room air conditioner) has its own compressor and refrigeration circuit. A CRAH (computer room air handler) uses chilled water from a central plant and a fan to move air across a coil. The choice affects efficiency, redundancy and how the rest of the plant is designed.

faqs.question: Is liquid cooling replacing air cooling?
faqs.answer: Not entirely. Liquid cooling is growing quickly for high-density racks, especially for AI hardware, but most facilities will run a mix of air and liquid cooling for years. The course covers both and how to decide which fits a given load.

faqs.question: How does cooling design affect PUE?
faqs.answer: PUE is total facility energy divided by IT energy, and cooling is usually the largest non-IT load. Containment, higher supply temperatures and economizer hours can all lower cooling energy and PUE. The final module ties these choices to energy costs.

faqs.question: What is the difference between RTO and RPO?
faqs.answer: RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore a service after a disruption. RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured as time since the last good copy. A service might have a four-hour RTO and a 15-minute RPO, for example.

faqs.question: What are hot, warm and cold sites?
faqs.answer: A hot site runs continuously and can take over almost immediately. A warm site has infrastructure in place but needs time to bring systems and data up to date. A cold site provides space and basic utilities only. Faster recovery costs more.

faqs.question: How often should a disaster recovery plan be tested?
faqs.answer: Most organizations test at least once a year and after significant changes, using a mix of tabletop exercises and technical failover tests. The DR Testing & Validation module covers how to design tests that show whether RTO and RPO targets are realistic.

faqs.question: What is integrated systems testing (IST)?
faqs.answer: IST is the final level of commissioning. It tests how power, cooling, controls and fire systems work together under realistic conditions, such as a utility failure with load banks simulating full IT load. It shows whether the facility actually rides through failures as designed.

faqs.question: What are superheat and subcooling?

faqs.question: What is the difference between single-mode and multimode fiber?
faqs.answer: Multimode fiber has a larger core and is used for shorter links, usually within a data hall. Single-mode fiber has a much smaller core and supports much longer distances, so it is used between buildings, campuses and increasingly inside large facilities for high-speed links.

faqs.question: What is an OTDR used for?
faqs.answer: An optical time-domain reflectometer sends light pulses into a fiber and measures what reflects back. It shows the location and loss of connectors, splices, bends and breaks along the link, which makes it the main tool for troubleshooting and documenting fiber runs.

faqs.question: Why are MPO/MTP connectors common in data centers?
faqs.answer: MPO/MTP connectors hold many fibers in one connector. They support the parallel optics used in many high-speed links and make high-density trunk cabling faster to install and reconfigure.

faqs.question: How is PUE calculated?
faqs.answer: PUE equals total facility energy divided by IT equipment energy over the same period. A PUE of 1.5 means that for every 1 kWh used by IT equipment, another 0.5 kWh goes to cooling, power losses and other overhead. Annual measurement gives the most meaningful comparison.

faqs.question: What is a good PUE?
faqs.answer: It depends on climate, design, age and load level. Large new facilities often design for PUEs well below 1.3, while many older or smaller sites run higher. Comparing your facility to its own history and to similar sites is more useful than a single target number.

faqs.question: Is PUE the only efficiency metric?
faqs.answer: No. PUE does not measure how efficiently IT equipment itself works, and it does not cover water or carbon. The Green Grid also defines WUE (water usage effectiveness) and CUE (carbon usage effectiveness), which many teams track alongside PUE.

faqs.question: What is the arc flash boundary?
faqs.answer: Under NFPA 70E, the arc flash boundary is the distance from exposed energized parts at which a person without arc-rated PPE could receive a second-degree burn, defined as an incident energy of 1.2 cal/cm². Anyone inside that boundary must wear PPE rated for the hazard.

faqs.question: What does an automatic transfer switch do?
faqs.answer: An ATS monitors the normal power source. When it fails, the ATS signals the generator to start and transfers the load once generator voltage and frequency are stable. When utility power returns, it transfers the load back and lets the generator cool down.

faqs.question: What is the difference between open and closed transition transfer?
faqs.answer: Open transition briefly disconnects the load before connecting it to the other source (break-before-make). Closed transition briefly parallels the two sources so the load is not interrupted (make-before-break), which requires additional controls and utility approval in many cases.

faqs.question: How often should standby generators be tested?
faqs.answer: NFPA 110 requires regular exercising and inspection, commonly monthly under load for Level 1 systems, plus periodic longer tests. The exact requirements depend on the system's classification and local rules, which the Maintenance for Readiness module explains.

faqs.question: What is thermal runaway?
faqs.answer: Thermal runaway is a chain reaction inside a battery cell where rising temperature causes reactions that release more heat. The cell can vent flammable and toxic gases and may ignite. In a battery module, heat can spread to neighboring cells.

faqs.question: How is a lithium-ion incident different from a lead-acid battery incident?
faqs.answer: Lead-acid batteries mainly pose hydrogen gas, electrolyte and electrical hazards. Lithium-ion batteries can go into self-sustaining thermal runaway, release large amounts of flammable gas quickly and reignite. Early detection and response planning are different as a result.

faqs.question: What should staff do if a lithium-ion battery alarm activates?
faqs.answer: Follow the facility's emergency procedure: evacuate the area if required, notify the fire department and site management, and avoid entering a room that may contain flammable gas. The course's response coordination module covers how to prepare these procedures.

faqs.question: What is OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart S?
faqs.answer: Subpart S is the electrical section of OSHA's general industry standards. It covers electrical installation requirements and, in 1910.331 through 1910.335, the safety-related work practices employers must follow to protect workers from electrical hazards.

faqs.question: Can data center technicians work on energized equipment?
faqs.answer: OSHA requires parts to be de-energized before work unless the employer can show that de-energizing creates greater hazards or is infeasible due to equipment design or operational limits. Energized work then requires qualified persons, safe work practices and appropriate PPE.

courses.summary: Core power distribution theory behind PDUs, panels, and branch circuits.
courses.description: Power distribution systems take facility-level power and break it down into the branch circuits that actually reach a rack. This course covers the fundamentals of that distribution chain: panels, breakers, PDUs, and load balancing, as the theory foundation for PDU architecture and monitoring work. You'll leave able to read a panel schedule, size a breaker correctly, and understand how distribution fundamentals show up in rack-level PDU design.
courses.why_it_matters: Between the UPS and the server power supply, electricity passes through switchboards, panelboards, power distribution units (PDUs), remote power panels and rack PDUs. Each step has breakers, ratings and limits. Mistakes here, such as an overloaded branch circuit, unbalanced phases or a dual-corded server plugged into the same feed twice, cause many avoidable outages. A key rule in data centers with A and B power feeds is that each side must be able to carry the full load if the other fails. That means each feed normally runs at well under half of its usable capacity. Breakers carrying continuous loads are also generally limited to 80% of their rating under the National Electrical Code. This course covers the distribution chain, panels and breaker sizing, load balancing and how these connect to PDU architecture.

faqs.question: Why should each side of an A/B power feed stay under 50%?
faqs.answer: In a redundant design, if one feed fails, the other must carry the entire load of dual-corded equipment. If each side is loaded above 50% of its usable capacity, the surviving side can trip on overload and cause an outage instead of preventing one.

faqs.question: What is phase balancing?
faqs.answer: Three-phase systems work best when load is spread evenly across the three phases. Unbalanced loads waste capacity, increase neutral current and can cause one phase to trip before the others. Load balancing is covered in its own module.

faqs.question: How often should a data center roof be inspected?
faqs.answer: A common practice is at least twice a year, often in spring and fall, plus after severe weather. Roofs with a lot of rooftop equipment or a history of leaks may need more frequent checks.

faqs.question: What are the most common causes of roof leaks?
faqs.answer: Failed flashing around penetrations and curbs, open seams, blocked drains that cause ponding, and punctures from foot traffic or dropped tools near rooftop equipment. Many of these can be found early with regular inspections.

faqs.question: How should roof repairs be prioritized?
faqs.answer: By risk: what is directly above critical equipment, how likely the defect is to leak and how bad the consequence would be. The course's risk-based prioritization module covers how to rank repairs so the most important work is done first.

faqs.question: How heavy is too heavy to lift alone?
faqs.answer: The NIOSH Revised Lifting Equation starts from 51 pounds under ideal conditions and reduces that limit for lifts that are far from the body, high, low, twisting or frequent. Many rack-mount lifts fall well below that adjusted limit, so team lifts or mechanical lifts are often needed.

faqs.question: When should a server lift be used?
faqs.answer: For heavy equipment, installations high or low in the rack, and any lift where the worker cannot keep the load close to the body. Many facilities set a weight threshold above which a lift or second person is required.

faqs.question: What is a double-conversion UPS?
faqs.answer: A double-conversion (online) UPS converts incoming AC power to DC and then back to clean AC for the load. The load is always fed by the inverter, so it is isolated from most utility disturbances, and there is no transfer time when utility power fails.

faqs.question: What do UPS modes like 'on bypass' and 'on battery' mean?
faqs.answer: 'On battery' means the UPS is supplying the load from its batteries because input power is lost or out of tolerance. 'On bypass' means the load is fed directly from the bypass source, not the inverter, so it is not protected by the batteries. The Control Panel & Alarms module explains these states.
